title: Saying who you are
seoTitle: Turkmen pronouns and the verb “to be”
intro: This unit is about people: the words for I, you, he and she, how to say what someone is (a student, tired, Turkmen) and where they are from. It also completes vowel harmony with rounding, and introduces the shorthand the guides use from now on for endings that change.

sections.title: High vowels and rounding: y, i, u, ü

blocks.text: The endings of [A1 unit 2](a1-u02) had *a* or *e*. Many other endings have a high vowel instead: *y*, *i*, *u* or *ü*. To choose, ask the question of unit 2 first: after a back vowel the ending has *y*, after a front vowel *i*. In this unit you will meet `-dyr` and `-dir`, and *-ly* and *-li*, as in *Aşgabatly* (from Ashgabat) and *Tejenli* (from Tejen).

Then comes rounding. The high vowel becomes *u* or *ü*, the rounded vowels, in just one place: when it is the vowel of the **second syllable** of the word, the **first** syllable has *o, ö, u* or *ü*, and it is **not the last letter** of the word. Everywhere else it stays *y* or *i*.

blocks.text: The words for **my** and **his** come in [A1 unit 9](a1-u09); here they only show the pattern. You will see it on many endings, so it pays to notice it now.

**The shorthand.** From now on, the guides write the changing vowel of an ending as a capital letter. **A** is *a* or *e*. **Y** is *y* or *i*, or *u* or *ü* where rounding applies. So the plural is `-lAr` (*-lar*, *-ler*), the ending in *Aşgabatly* is `-lY` (*-ly*, *-li*…), and the ending you meet in this unit is `-dYr` (*-dyr*, *-dir*…).

blocks.label: The shorthand
lines: A  =  a after a back vowel, e after a front vowel
Y  =  y after a back vowel, i after a front vowel
Y  =  u or ü in the second syllable after o, ö, u or ü, unless it ends the word

blocks.text: Rounding never touches **A**: *gözler* (eyes), *öýler* (houses), never *gözlör*. And a vowel at the very end of a word stays unrounded: *gözi*, not *gözü*.

sections.title: I, you, he, she: the personal pronouns

head: Pronoun
Meaning
rows: you (several people, or one person, politely)

blocks.text: There is no gender: *ol* means he, she or it, and the context tells you which. *ol* and *olar* are the same words as **that** and **those** in [A1 unit 2](a1-u02): *ol kitap* is that book, *Ol mugallym* is he or she is a teacher.

**sen or siz?** Use *sen* with a friend, a child, or a relative of your own age or younger. Use *siz* with anyone older, with people you don't know well, at work, and with several people. When in doubt, use *siz*: being too polite is rarely a mistake. If someone calls you *sen*, that doesn't mean you should answer with *sen*.

items.en: He is a doctor. / She is a doctor.

blocks.text: **When the pronoun stays.** In the short form of **to be** (next section), nothing else in the sentence shows who is meant, so the pronoun has to be there: *Men talyp* is I am a student, but *Talyp.* on its own is just “a student”. When a word carries a personal ending, as verbs do from [A1 unit 6](a1-u06), the pronoun can be left out.
Notice that the noun after *biz*, *siz* or *olar* can stay singular: *Biz okuwçy*, we are pupils. After *olar* you will also hear the plural: *Olar talyplar*.

In the present, Turkmen usually says **to be** with no word at all. Put the subject and what it is side by side, whether that is a job, a nationality or a feeling. This short form works in every person, and it is the one you will hear most:

rows.en: he or she is a student
you are students; you are a student (polite)

blocks.text: **-dYr in the third person.** In careful speech and in writing, *ol* and *olar* often add `-dYr` (*-dyr*, *-dir*, *-dur*, *-dür*). It makes the statement sound firmer, a little like “she is indeed a teacher”, and it is common in written facts and descriptions. With *olar* it is *-dYr* or *-dYrlAr*.

**The formal written form.** In formal writing, letters and speeches, you will also see `-dYr` followed by a personal ending in the first and second persons: *Men talypdyryn* (I am a student), *Biz minnetdardyrys* (we are grateful). You don't need these forms to speak, but you should recognize them. The endings are the ones the present tense of verbs uses in [A1 unit 6](a1-u06):

rows.en: he or she is a student
you are students; you are a student (polite)

blocks.title: Keep the subject
blocks.text: With the short form, the pronoun or name must be there: *Men talyp*, never just *Talyp* for **I am a student**. With an ending, it can go: *Talypdyryn* already says **I**.

blocks.title: No bir with jobs
blocks.text: Say *Men mugallym* (I am a teacher), without *bir*. **Not** and questions with **to be** (*Men talyp däl*, *Sen talypmy?*) come in [A1 unit 4](a1-u04).

sections.title: Nationalities and where you are from

blocks.text: Nationality words are nouns, and they are written in lowercase: *türkmen* (a Turkmen), *rus* (a Russian), *iňlis* (an English person), *nemes* (a German), *fransuz* (a French person), *özbek* (an Uzbek), *gazak* (a Kazakh). Use them like jobs, with the short form of **to be**: *Men türkmen*, I am Turkmen.

**From a town.** To ask where someone is from, say *Siz nireli?* (or *Sen nireli?*). Answer with the name of your town and the ending `-lY` (*-ly*, *-li*): *Men Aşgabatly*, I am from Ashgabat. Use it as a set pattern for now; the ending itself is taught in [A2 unit 12](a2-u12).
Nationality words take no capital: *türkmen*, *iňlis*. Names of countries and towns do: *Türkmenistan*, *Angliýa*, *Aşgabat*.

summary: Endings with a high vowel have *y* after back vowels and *i* after front ones; *u* or *ü* only in the second syllable after *o, ö, u, ü*, and never at the end of a word: *gözüm*, but *gözi*.
From now on, **A** stands for *a/e* and **Y** for *y/i/u/ü*: `-lAr`, `-dYr`, `-lY`.
The pronouns are *men, sen, ol, biz, siz, olar*. *ol* is he, she and it; *siz* is plural, and polite for one person.
In the present, **to be** usually has no word: *Men talyp*. The pronoun must then be said.
In careful style the third person adds `-dYr`: *Ol mugallymdyr*. Formal writing adds `-dYr` with an ending in every person: *Men talypdyryn*.
Nationality words are lowercase nouns: *Men türkmen*. *Siz nireli?* asks where someone is from: *Men Aşgabatly*.
